system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2188-05-15 02:19:00 to 2188-05-16 11:35:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex history including sclerosing mesenteritis, multiple abdominal surgeries, and chronic anemia was admitted for vomiting, diarrhea, and new-onset bright red blood per rectum. Her hemoglobin had progressively dropped from 8.5 to 7.4 g/dL, prompting admission. Stool studies were negative for infection, and an abdominal X-ray showed dilated bowel loops without obstruction. A flexible sigmoidoscopy revealed no active bleeding source or ulcers, with findings suggesting resolved rectal lesions. Despite IV iron infusion, her hemoglobin continued to decline, necessitating transfusion of 2 units of packed red blood cells, after which her levels stabilized at 9.0 g/dL. Pain was managed conservatively due to prior sedation with opioids. She was discharged home in stable condition with plans for outpatient GI follow-up, including possible capsule endoscopy, and instructions to monitor for recurrent bleeding.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you here at ___ 
___. You were admitted to our hospital 
after suspect of surgical site infection after closure of your 
gastrocutaneous fistula. Please follow the recommendations below 
to ensure a speedy and uneventful recovery.

ACTIVITY:
 - Do not drive until you have stopped taking pain medicine and 
feel you could respond in an emergency.
 - You may go outside, but avoid traveling long distances until 
you see your surgeon at your next visit.
 - You may start some light exercise when you feel comfortable.
 - You will need to stay out of bathtubs or swimming pools for a 
time while your incision is healing. Ask your doctor when you 
can resume tub baths or swimming.

YOUR INCISION:
 - Your incision may be slightly red around the edges. This is 
normal.
 - Your incision is packed and will heal from the bottom up. You 
will have a visiting nurse to help you with your wound. 
 - It is normal to feel a firm ridge along the incision. This 
will go away.
 - You may see a small amount of clear or light red fluid 
staining your dressing or clothes. If the staining is severe, 
please call your surgeon.
 - Over the next ___ months, your incision will fade and become 
less prominent.

YOUR BOWELS:
 - Constipation is a common side effect of medicine such as 
Percocet or codeine. If needed, you may take a stool softener 
(such as Colace, one capsule) or gentle laxative (such as milk 
of magnesia, 1 tbs) twice a day. You can get both of these 
medicines without a prescription.
 - If you go 48 hours without a bowel movement, or have pain 
moving the bowels, call your surgeon.
 - After some operations, diarrhea can occur. If you get 
diarrhea, don't take anti-diarrhea medicines. Drink plenty of 
fluids and see if it goes away. If it does not go away, or is 
severe and you feel ill, please call your surgeon.

PAIN MANAGEMENT:
 - It is normal to feel some discomfort/pain following abdominal 
surgery. This pain is often described as ""soreness"".
 - Your pain should get better day by day. If you find the pain 
is getting worse instead of better, please contact your surgeon.
 -You will receive a prescription from your surgeon for pain 
medicine to take by mouth. It is important to take this medicine 
as directed.
 - Do not take it more frequently than prescribed. Do not take 
more medicine at one time than prescribed.
 - Your pain medicine will work better if you take it before 
your pain gets too severe.
 - Talk with your surgeon about how long you will need to take 
prescription pain medicine. Please don't take any other pain 
medicine, including non-prescription pain medicine, unless your 
surgeon has said its okay.
 - If you are experiencing no pain, it is okay to skip a dose of 
pain medicine.
 - Remember to use your ""cough pillow"" for splinting when you 
cough or when you are doing your deep breathing exercises.
 If you experience any of the following, please contact your 
surgeon:
 - sharp pain or any severe pain that lasts several hours
 - pain that is getting worse over time
 - pain accompanied by fever of more than 101
 - a drastic change in nature or quality of your pain
 
MEDICATIONS:
 - Take all the medicines you were on before the operation just 
as you did before, unless you have been told differently.
 - If you have any questions about what medicine to take or not 
to take, please call your surgeon.

less prominent.

YOUR BOWELS:
 - Constipation is a common side effect of medicine such as 
Percocet or codeine. If needed, you may take a stool softener 
(such as Colace, one capsule) or gentle laxative (such as milk 
of magnesia, 1 tbs) twice a day. You can get both of these 
medicines without a prescription.
 - If you go 48 hours without a bowel movement, or have pain 
moving the bowels, call your surgeon.
 - After some operations, diarrhea can occur. If you get 
diarrhea, don't take anti-diarrhea medicines. Drink plenty of 
fluids and see if it goes away. If it does not go away, or is 
severe and you feel ill, please call your surgeon.

PAIN MANAGEMENT:
 - It is normal to feel some discomfort/pain following abdominal 
surgery. This pain is often described as ""soreness"".
 - Your pain should get better day by day. If you find the pain 
is getting worse instead of better, please contact your surgeon.
 -You will receive a prescription from your surgeon for pain 
medicine to take by mouth. It is important to take this medicine 
as directed.
 - Do not take it more frequently than prescribed. Do not take 
more medicine at one time than prescribed.
 - Your pain medicine will work better if you take it before 
your pain gets too severe.
 - Talk with your surgeon about how long you will need to take 
prescription pain medicine. Please don't take any other pain 
medicine, including non-prescription pain medicine, unless your 
surgeon has said its okay.
 - If you are experiencing no pain, it is okay to skip a dose of 
pain medicine.
 - Remember to use your ""cough pillow"" for splinting when you 
cough or when you are doing your deep breathing exercises.
 If you experience any of the following, please contact your 
surgeon:
 - sharp pain or any severe pain that lasts several hours
 - pain that is getting worse over time
 - pain accompanied by fever of more than 101
 - a drastic change in nature or quality of your pain
 
MEDICATIONS:
 - Take all the medicines you were on before the operation just 
as you did before, unless you have been told differently.
 - If you have any questions about what medicine to take or not 
to take, please call your surgeon.

 
Followup Instructions:
___

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with increasing pain and redness around your surgical site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started two days ago. The area’s getting more tender, and the redness is spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You had the gastrocutaneous fistula closure five days ago, correct? And the wound was dry until now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was healing fine. No drainage. But now it’s warm, swollen, and really sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You don’t have a fever or chills, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’ve been afebrile. Just the local pain and redness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Given your history of MRSA, we’re going to start you on vancomycin and get some imaging to make sure the infection isn’t deeper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see what the CT shows. If it’s just superficial, we may just need to drain it at the bedside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is back. There’s a small fluid collection, but it’s superficial—no connection to the abdominal cavity. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do a bedside incision and drainage to remove the infected fluid. It’s a quick procedure, and you’ll be awake with local anesthesia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll feel some pressure, but we’ll numb the area well. Afterward, we’ll pack the wound so it heals from the inside out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Procedure went smoothly. We drained a small amount of pus and packed the wound. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Is the packing going to be painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might feel a bit uncomfortable, but we’ll manage your pain with IV Dilaudid as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also worried about the E. coli we saw in the swab. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture showed E. coli and Proteus, both sensitive to the antibiotics we’re using. Vancomycin covers MRSA, but we’ll adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But vancomycin isn’t for E. coli, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're right. We started vancomycin for MRSA coverage. Since the infection is superficial and the organisms are sensitive, we may switch or stop antibiotics soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The microbiology report confirms E. coli and Proteus vulgaris, both sensitive to several antibiotics. We’ll continue monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to stay on antibiotics long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. Since the infection is localized and improving, we’ll stop antibiotics once the wound looks clean. Healing will be by secondary intention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today? On a scale of 1 to 10?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About a 4 now. Much better since the drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll switch you to oral pain meds soon. Also, your labs show mild anemia—Hgb 7.5—but stable, so no transfusion needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s been chronic for years. I’m used to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history shows anemia of chronic disease. We’ll manage it outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound is looking much better—less redness and swelling. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need help with the dressing at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A visiting nurse will assist initially, but you said you’re comfortable changing it yourself. We’ll teach you the steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the packing—how long will that continue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until the wound heals from the bottom up—could take weeks. You’ll taper packing as it fills in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What signs should I watch for that mean I need to come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever over 101, increasing redness or pain, foul-smelling drainage, or if the wound opens widely. Also, no bowel movement in 48 hours—given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—can I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your pre-admission meds except painkillers you’re allergic to. We’ve added rabeprazole for reflux and acetaminophen for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I don’t need more antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given the wound improvement and superficial nature, we’re stopping antibiotics. The body can handle the rest with proper wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Follow up with your surgeon in one week. Call sooner if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and keep up with the wound care. You’re healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll avoid driving until I’m off pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Safety first. See you in clinic.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex surgical history, including sclerosing mesenteritis and prior gastrocutaneous fistula, was admitted five days after surgical closure due to increasing pain, erythema, and induration at the incision site. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Imaging revealed a superficial fluid collection, and bedside incision and drainage were performed. Cultures grew Escherichia coli and Proteus vulgaris, both sensitive to antibiotics. She was initially treated with vancomycin for MRSA prophylaxis, but antibiotics were discontinued due to clinical improvement and superficial healing by secondary intention. Pain was managed with IV Dilaudid, then transitioned to acetaminophen. She was discharged home with wound care instructions, a visiting nurse, and follow-up planned. No further antibiotics were prescribed.
